video_title: Live from Georgetown University: AI Policy in 2027 with Alexandra Reeve Givens
gist: At a live Scaling Laws/Lawfare event at Georgetown, CDT CEO Alexandra Reeve Givens and Alex Bores (Who Decides) argue the 2026 midterms, driven by affordability and the data-center backlash, made AI a mainstream political issue, setting up frontier-safety legislation (incident reporting, independent audits, RAISE Act-style rules) in the next Congress, aggressive bipartisan state AG enforcement (e.g., a $25B New Mexico-Meta settlement), and state-level copycat laws. They push back on the post-election narrative that Democratic gains and regulation are bad for AI stocks, and flag lab timelines for automating AI research as early as 2027.

insights.claim: Alexandra Reeve Givens says the 2026 midterm was primarily an affordability election, but the data-center fight was its strongest tech-policy component, reflecting voters' sense that tech was imposing projects on communities without a seat at the table or local benefit.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Reeve Givens
insights.so_what: Local opposition is a rising permitting and political risk for data-center developers, utilities and hyperscaler capex plans.
insights.quote: This is tech foisting something on communities without them having a seat at the table

insights.claim: Givens cites Jon Ossoff's acceptance speech attacking tech titans building bunkers in New Zealand while saying AI could kill people, as evidence that anti-tech-elite rhetoric is now a winning campaign theme.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Reeve Givens
insights.so_what: Expect AI companies to face hostile messaging from newly empowered Democrats.

insights.claim: The host notes OpenAI's Chris Lehane put out a memo saying the 2028 election will definitely be the AI election.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Labs expect AI to be a central 2028 campaign issue and are preparing politically.
insights.quote: Chris Lehane of OpenAI put out a memo saying the 2028 election will definitely be the AI election.

insights.claim: The election produced six or seven new Democratic trifectas at the state level, making states more internally aligned on AI policy even as they diverge from one another.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Expect a wave of state AI bills in 2027 sessions in Democratic-controlled states.
insights.quote: this election that has produced six or seven new Democratic trifectas

insights.claim: Givens says a post-election narrative that Democrats taking power crashed AI companies' stock values was a market overreaction, since corrected, and that reasonable regulation helps durable AI adoption rather than stifling it.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Reeve Givens
insights.so_what: Suggests post-election AI selloffs on regulatory fear may be buying opportunities; regulation risk is being over-discounted.
insights.quote: It was the market overreacting.

insights.claim: Alex Bores jokes that since the election the labs have suddenly become strongly Democrat-aligned, and says industry now feels something very powerful is coming soon and, despite past opposition, that government action is needed, mixed with doubt that government is up to it.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Labs pivoting toward accepting regulation lowers odds of a protracted lobbying war and could produce industry-shaped rules.
insights.quote: They're suddenly very strongly and always have been Democrat aligned, it turns out.

insights.claim: Before the election the Trump administration launched a superintelligence task force coordinating lab reporting and consumer-protection enforcement, and after the election there was a chief-of-staff change and a shift in tone; Givens says whether Trump's approach changes is undecided.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host) / Alexandra Reeve Givens
insights.so_what: Federal AI oversight direction is in flux; watch agency staffing and task-force outputs.

insights.claim: Givens credits the administration's voluntary accord with labs for meaningful commitments on board governance, independent auditing and evaluation, and incident reporting, but says voluntary commitments on a subset of companies must soon become a rigorous regime applied consistently.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Reeve Givens
insights.so_what: Mandatory third-party audit and incident reporting regimes are coming; positive for AI assurance/evaluation vendors, a compliance cost for labs.
insights.quote: the call for independent auditing and evaluation so the companies aren't just grading their own homework

insights.claim: Givens says the White House's framework governing which AI models can be released is still secret; CDT has filed a FOIA request, and she argues a company's success should not rise or fall on White House whims.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Reeve Givens
insights.so_what: An undisclosed federal release-gating regime is a material, opaque political risk for lab valuations and launch timing.
insights.quote: In what world does it make sense that there's a secret regime deciding what models can be released for the public or not?

insights.claim: Givens predicts frontier safety will stay top of mind in Congress because real AI-enabled cybersecurity incidents, like those over the summer, will keep recurring; Hakeem Jeffries convened a meeting so work can start in the lame duck.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Reeve Givens
insights.so_what: Frontier-AI legislation could move as soon as the lame-duck session; cybersecurity incidents are the catalyst to watch.
insights.quote: I firmly believe we're going to keep seeing incidents like some of the cybersecurity incidents we saw over the summer.

insights.claim: California is developing recommendations under Governor Newsom's executive order on independent auditing, embedded evaluators and incident-reporting regimes, which Givens sees as a source for federal legislative proposals alongside the RAISE Act.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Reeve Givens
insights.so_what: California's audit/incident framework is likely the template for national rules.

insights.claim: Givens argues AI governance is shaped by multiple levers beyond legislation, including oversight, litigation, and private markets via what can be insured and contract disputes.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Reeve Givens
insights.so_what: Insurability of AI risk is an emerging market-driven governance channel to watch for insurers.
insights.quote: what can get insured, what can't get insured

insights.claim: The host says AI has become as broad a policy issue as the economy, and federal legislating has been reduced to a few big reconciliation bills or unanimous-consent items, leaving states as the only level to pass significant AI regulation.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk for AI firms is concentrated in state law for now.
insights.quote: It's states are the only level that has really passed significant regulations on AI.

insights.claim: The host notes Senate confirmations may increasingly vet nominees on their AI positions, and agency minutiae will be a subtle signal of administration shifts.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Confirmation hearings become a venue for AI policy signals.

themes.theme: States and AGs as AI enforcers

insights.claim: Givens expects convergence rather than a patchwork in state AI laws, as states copy well-baked models; she cites California's newly passed 'No Robo Bosses' law on AI in workplace decisions as one others may copy.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Reeve Givens
insights.so_what: HR-tech and AI hiring tools face spreading compliance obligations across states.
insights.quote: On these issues, I actually think we're going to start seeing more convergence

insights.claim: Givens says state attorneys general are 'running the table' on tech policy, citing a $25 billion New Mexico settlement with Meta directed to education and a state settlement with General Motors over reselling drivers' data to two data brokers; the enforcement is bipartisan.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Reeve Givens
insights.so_what: Large AG settlements are a material, recurring liability for big tech and data-monetizing firms; price in consumer-protection enforcement risk.
insights.quote: The state AGs are actually running the table in shaping tech policy in this time period.

insights.claim: States facing budget crises want tech-policy proposals that improve state finances, favoring measures that are cheap to administer or revenue-generating.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Reeve Givens
insights.so_what: Expect revenue-raising tech measures (settlements, fees, taxes) to gain traction at state level.
insights.quote: they're actually looking for proposals that are going to make a net difference to the state's coffers

insights.claim: The host says state lobbying is dominated by a few contract lobbyists representing big interests, leaving civil society underrepresented.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Industry retains influence at the state level, moderating outcomes.

insights.claim: Givens disputes the idea of 'boring AI', noting government chatbots carry big human-impact risks: a New York pilot chatbot advised businesses how to avoid regulations, and the host notes the Philadelphia Police Department has received fake murder tips from AI chatbots.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Reeve Givens / Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Public-sector AI deployments carry reputational and liability risk; vendors may need sandboxes and testing.
insights.quote: Is it directing them to break the law as happened in a pilot in New York

insights.claim: The host cites Bank of America data that just 3.3% of American households had a paid AI subscription, arguing low trust limits adoption and that labs must address public sentiment.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Consumer AI monetization remains early; trust-building and regulation may be prerequisites for subscription growth.
insights.quote: Bank of America said just 3.3% of American households had a paid subscription to AI.

insights.claim: About 75 days after a major AI incident referred to as 'Hugging Face', OpenAI announced a 'control room' mechanism to detect evaluations going off the rails and block certain jobs, which the host reads as labs racing to pre-empt public pressure.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Labs are investing in self-regulatory safety controls ahead of IPOs and legislation.
insights.quote: OpenAI most recently announced their new control room

insights.claim: The host notes several labs are nearing IPOs and jokes listeners may soon hold shares in Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Upcoming AI lab IPOs make regulatory and safety-incident risk directly investable.
insights.quote: even as many of them near IPOs.

insights.claim: Bores says AI companies all aim to fully automate AI research (recursive self-improvement): OpenAI estimated March 2028, Anthropic employees say 2027, and AI Futures and a new METR report suggest 2027 may be more accurate.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Near-term automation-of-research timelines drive both AI capex bull cases and the urgency of regulation.
insights.quote: So OpenAI estimated they'd get there March of 2028, Anthropic employees say 2027

insights.claim: CDT built 'Selective Memory', a tool for porting only chosen parts of chatbot history between providers like Anthropic, OpenAI or open models, in two days, to show that selective data portability is easy and companies should offer it.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Reeve Givens
insights.so_what: Portability mandates would reduce chatbot switching costs and lock-in, pressuring consumer AI pricing.
insights.quote: We should be able to have selective portability.

insights.claim: Current AI piloted a $2 offline handheld device that translates speech between languages in real time using only open-source tools, built in about two months before last year's India AI Summit.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Reeve Givens
insights.so_what: Open-source stacks enable ultra-cheap edge AI devices, a potential low-cost competitive threat in emerging markets.

insights.claim: Givens says AI is reshaping democracy via information mediation (feeds, deepfakes, Google AI summaries), surveillance such as ICE using face recognition to track protesters to their homes in the past year, and concentrated wealth, and expects big-money attempts to sway the 2028 elections.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Reeve Givens
insights.so_what: Facial recognition and surveillance tech face growing political and legal backlash risk.
insights.quote: ICE tracking down protesters and following to their them to their home because they've done face recognition is not a hypothetical.

insights.claim: Givens argues frontier-only focus ignores privacy risks from reliance on chatbots and agents, and AI decisions on healthcare, insurance, jobs and benefits, which she expects Congress and states to address sector by sector.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Reeve Givens
insights.so_what: Sector-specific AI rules in insurance, health and employment are likely; vertical AI vendors should expect compliance burdens.
